title: Specify separate convenience and throughput contracts, including incremental background messages
body:
# Convenience and throughput contracts

**Rust interface sketch for feedback:** [review page](https://github.com/servil-software-factory/BLAKE3/blob/design/stream-api/docs/api-sketch.md), with discussion in [the draft review PR](https://github.com/servil-software-factory/BLAKE3/pull/275). Names and lifetimes are provisional.

Proposed contract, November 6, 2026. This specifies the replacement for the shared dual-purpose Hasher. Current code keeps its existing behavior until implementation and callers change together.

Convenience owns input preparation and returns synchronous results. Throughput makes preparation explicit and supplies efficient ready-bulk execution and an incremental background pipeline. Incremental input belongs in both contracts. Background progress belongs in the throughput pipeline.

## 1. Convenience

Purpose: hash ordinary application bytes with straightforward call/return semantics.

- Accept ordinary byte slices with arbitrary alignment and lengths. The library owns any staging and final-block preparation.
- Provide one-shot hashing and `convenience::Hasher` for one message supplied across many calls. Plain hashing, keyed hashing, key derivation and extended output remain available. Unknown-length message construction/reset accepts an optional advisory total-length hint, specified below.
- `update(bytes)` incorporates the bytes in order. After return the caller may immediately overwrite or release that input. The Hasher owns all state and retained bytes it needs.
- `finalize()` returns the hash of the bytes supplied so far. Finalization remains repeatable. Copying/checkpointing state stays a convenience operation.
- Calls are synchronous and leave no hashing job referring to the caller's input. This family exposes no background-submit or parallel-update variant.
- Use the calling thread, including hardware instructions on that core. Library worker startup and pipeline storage are outside this contract.
- Tune for calls amid other work. The API identifies this pattern.

## 2. Throughput input contract

Keep the prepared-input decision in [#260](https://github.com/servil-software-factory/BLAKE3/issues/260) (prepared types for throughput inputs).

Purpose: give the hashing implementation prepared data and preserve its fast paths.

- Core hashing entry points accept prepared types. The producer owns any alignment/padding preparation before submission.
- `Block` establishes 64-byte alignment and whole-block storage. Its contents need not be zero. Existing calls that ignore bytes past a logical end retain that meaning. `Batch` also establishes logical message lengths and zero padding after every message.
- A new incremental-input type carries complete non-final algorithm chunks, or a final portion with its logical length, accessible rounded storage and zero tail. Preparation helpers enforce these properties. Producers work with buffers and ready input, leaving internal chunk/job sizes to those helpers.
- A producer can receive or generate bytes directly into a preparation buffer across several callbacks. Preparing its ready prefix or final portion is explicit producer work. The hashing operation consumes only the resulting prepared view.
- Preparation and submission are distinct ownership steps. Hashing leaves retained input immutable. Typed leases or scoped borrows prevent overwrite and reuse until returned.
- A whole ready message is one prepared input followed by end-of-message. A `Batch` is the compact prepared form for a group of complete equal-length messages. Its known layout may select a specialized kernel directly.

The value is always BLAKE3 of the logical bytes in order, independent of packet boundaries, preparation-buffer boundaries and worker assignments. Padding contributes no logical bytes. Control flow and memory access depend on public input shapes, independently of key and message values.

## 3. Incremental background pipeline

Use one throughput stream/engine, with one write handle for each unfinished message. Multiple handles can be active and interleaved. A single Mode is fixed for the stream, as today. Operation names below describe semantics. Spelling and Rust lifetimes remain implementation work.

| Operation | Contract |
|---|---|
| Begin a message | Await a reserved message slot, then associate its output place and caller tag and return the sole write handle. The total length may be unknown. Accept an optional advisory total-length hint. |
| Obtain writable input | Await a preparation buffer with its submission capacity already reserved. Receive/generate bytes directly into it, across callbacks if needed. |
| Commit prepared input | Commit ready portions of a reserved buffer immediately, preserving a partial portion for further preparation. Submission succeeds without another capacity check and returns without waiting for hashing. |
| Send existing prepared input | Await admission and transfer the entire prepared input without a repair copy. Complete the send when accepted, independently of digest completion. |
| End a message | Commit its reserved final prepared portion and declare the input complete. Consume the write handle and return without waiting for hashing. Ending with no final bytes needs no new input capacity. |
| Abort a message | Stop accepting its bytes and produce no digest. Skip queued work for it; bounded jobs already running may finish before its storage returns. Other messages proceed. Recording abort requires no new input capacity. |
| Receive completions | Return available results and freed input places. A caller can inspect ready completions or await a registered notification. |
| Finish/drain | Require every message ended or aborted, then wait for all accepted work and deliver the remaining completions. This is the explicit wait for hashing completion. |

### Backpressure: request once, receive reserved capacity

Capacity flows back to the producer as a reserved buffer or admission grant. A capacity request completes immediately when space is available. Otherwise the engine registers that request once. When space returns, the engine reserves it for an eligible waiter before notifying that producer. The producer receives usable capacity, not an invitation to race for it again.

- Rust exposes this as a runtime-independent awaitable operation. An event-loop adapter delivers a grant notification. A blocking reader sleeps on the same request. Each uses the same reservation mechanism.
- An available-capacity request takes the immediate path, without waiter registration or a wakeup. Pending request bookkeeping uses preallocated or caller-owned storage, preserving the allocation contract. Re-polling a pending request reuses its waiter record.
- Registration and the capacity recheck prevent lost wakeups. Only waiters with granted capacity need notification. Notifications for one producer can be coalesced.
- Serve requests in arrival order for each capacity kind. Message-slot and input-buffer requests have independent wait queues, so a new message cannot block existing messages from obtaining input capacity and completing.
- Cancellation removes a pending request or returns its unconsumed grant. Aborting a message cancels its pending input request. Already accepted input follows the normal worker-release rules.
- Preparation helpers seal ready portions into the required prepared types before commit. A reservation covers input storage/admission and the queue metadata needed to accept it. Receiving a short fragment preserves the partial preparation state for the next receive.

Ordinary backpressure exposes an awaitable grant, with sleeping or event-loop notification supplied by the API. The caller resumes when it owns capacity. A capacity grant promises admission, not completion of the hash.

Further guarantees:

- Constructing the engine reserves its configured submission storage and metadata. Producer control operations reuse them without per-packet heap allocation. Input allocation/preparation remains explicit producer work.
- Accepted work progresses with the configured workers while the producer is doing other work. Progress requires neither another packet nor a subsequent submission.
- Ordering is per message. An unfinished or slow message does not withhold an unrelated message's completed result. Output ownership returns exactly once on success. Abort returns the place with no digest.
- Each input place returns when its jobs and retained boundary data have been consumed, allowing buffer reuse before the message ends.
- The engine handles empty messages and ends on block/chunk boundaries, retaining the boundary state it needs. Ending requires only the final portion and existing state.
- The producer chooses its data flow, leaving worker-job sizes and kernels to the library. The library batches useful work and spreads a long message across cores where that helps. Its paths are tuned for ongoing work, including the real producer gaps the benchmark measures.
- No CPU work is performed merely in anticipation of input that has not arrived. With no runnable accepted work, workers sleep.

## 4. Budgets and the ready-bulk fast path

- Retain the process-wide pool and its current count. A configured N includes one caller participant and permits N−1 shared library workers. Application producer threads remain caller-owned. The background pipeline requires at least one worker (N ≥ 2). A caller-only configuration supports direct prepared bulk work.
- Bound retained input and message slots, counting granted/reserved capacity and library-owned preparation buffers too. Exhausted capacity queues an admission request while the producer sleeps or handles other events. An input must fit the total capacity. An oversized input is a precondition error, detected before waiting. Preparation helpers produce admissible sizes.
- Keep a direct prepared-bulk execution path for already-ready work. It returns completed results and supports caller-only execution. Pipeline setup, callback traffic and worker wakeups each need a measured benefit in that path. Static input forms can preserve these shortcuts.
- Public bulk operations and pipeline operations have different wait points but one throughput purpose. Remove redundant spelling only where measurements show the replacement preserves their time, CPU, memory and allocation contracts.
- GPU selection stays internal wherever it improves efficiency within the caller's execution budget. Caller-only hashing stays on its CPU core.

## 5. Optional advisory length hints

Every unknown-length message-start operation accepts `length_hint: Option<u64>`. This includes convenience Hasher construction/reset, throughput message creation and reader/fill adapters that start a message. Adapters attached to an existing message use its stored hint, leaving ordinary feeds unchanged.

- The estimate is the likely total logical message length in bytes. `None` means unknown. Every `u64` value, including zero, is valid advice.
- The hint may guide bounded buffering, batching, scheduling and backend selection. It stays within the configured memory and worker budgets, including when the estimate is enormous.
- Accepted bytes and explicit end-of-message determine the digest. A hint neither supplies bytes nor limits their count. A short source ends normally, and a source longer than the estimate continues normally.
- End-of-message flushes the work needed for completion regardless of the estimate. Completion depends on actual input and end-of-message alone.
- Reset starts a fresh message with its supplied hint, clearing the previous hint when given `None`.
- C exposes the same optional value and semantics. Equal actual bytes produce equal output with no hint, a low estimate, an exact estimate or a high estimate.

## 6. Ownership, failures and scope

- Rust types tie a message to its engine and consume its write handle on end/abort. Compile-fail examples cover cross-engine handles, append-after-end and reuse of retained storage.
- A scope ends only after drain. Shutdown correctness does not depend on a destructor racing outstanding borrowed work. Panic across an active borrowed-work scope stops the process, as current streams do.
- I/O errors and protocol disconnects are normal producer events: explicitly abort that message and continue other work.
- A broken input invariant, foreign handle or lifecycle precondition fails stop with its cause. The implementation does not repair misuse by copying or switching execution modes.
- Completion handlers run on the producer's polling/draining thread. Workers signal readiness and compute hashes.
- The public C API exposes convenience hashing only: ordinary bytes, synchronous one-shot/incremental hashing, modes and extended output. Unknown-length C Hasher construction/reset accepts the same optional advisory total-length hint.
- Prepared bulk inputs, background ingestion, buffer reservations, wakeups, library-managed multithreading and GPU use stay Rust-only. Remove the existing C multithreaded/stream exports and update their callers at migration. Internal C/assembly kernel interfaces remain unchanged.

## 7. Acceptance work

Before migration, add the missing receive-and-hash use case to the benchmark contract. Compare whole resulting implementations.

- One long message in small irregular fragments, with producer work/gaps between arrivals. Several interleaved unfinished messages. Ready prepared messages and batches.
- Known and unknown total lengths, empty input, exact boundaries, final partial input, admission waiting and disconnect/abort. Exercise no hint, zero, underestimates, exact estimates, overestimates and the maximum hint.
- Verify overlap with a deterministic handshake: committing a granted buffer returns while a worker is deliberately held. A planted wait-for-hash mutation must fail it.
- Hold a consumer to exhaust capacity. Check one registered request, a reserved grant before notification, successful commit after wakeup, cancellation and independent progress of message-slot/input-buffer waiters. Plant a lost wakeup and a stolen-grant fault so the controls demonstrate these failures.
- Check actual digest values, guard pages, type/lifetime misuse, bounded memory and progress of unrelated completed messages.
- Preserve the direct prepared-bulk performance cases and the convenience cases. Preparation copies are charged where a caller needs them. Direct producers retain their zero-copy route.
- Measure wall time and hardware counters through clocks, with current paired judgments and native Mac before VM timing. Gate shared Rust paths on the other supported machines.

Implement the new contract by improving/replacing the existing stream engine. The convenience Hasher keeps synchronous incremental state. The throughput message handle owns pipeline submission. Shared compression and tree logic remain private where sharing costs the throughput path nothing.

Specification only. Correctness, mutation and speed runs are deferred to implementation because this proposal changes no compiled code. Prose checked with claudish. “Exactly once” names the output ownership guarantee.

— John Servil
